Brutal Legacy

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
the biggest threat to South African women come from their own partners. Why cant South Africa reduce stop this terrible crime

Unique Selling Point:
Powerful personal stories well told. Footage from the Oscar Trial - startling statistics. Unsung heroines

Summary:
"As I stood before him all I could see were the lies, the disappearing for days without warning, the screaming, the threats, the terror, the hostage-holding, the keeping me up all night, the dragging me through the house by my hair, the choking, the doors locked around me, the phones disconnected, the isolation, the fear and the uncertainty."

A new book, Brutal Legacy, by former newsreader Tracy Going tells about the night she thought she would die at the hands of her partner. The book comes at a time that Karabo Mokoena's partner stands trial for her murder and Constantia business man Rob Packham is accused of murdering his wife Gill. Both women's bodies found, charred beyond recognition.


Further information:
Tracy Going survived the attack when neighbours intervened, but the scars remained. When Oscar killed his girlfriend Reeva, Tracy spent obsessive hours watching the channel and came close to a nervous breakdown. To heal herself she began to write her story. It is a searing account of abuse in the home, first by first her father and later her partner

"I was ashamed of my father, the drunk. If he wasn't throwing back the liquid in the lounge then he'd be finding comfort and consort in his cans at the golf club. With that came the uncertainty as I lay in my bed and waited for him to return. I would lie there holding my curtain tight in my small hand. I would pull the fabric down, almost straight, forming a strained sliver and I would peer into the blackness, unblinking. It seemed I was always watching and waiting. Sometimes I searched for satellites between the twinkles of light, but mostly the fear in my tummy distracted me."

One woman every eight hours dies at the hands of her partner. In Canada for example its one every six days. Despite nearly 20 years of government legislation and awareness campaigns to reduce domestic violence, South African women are still more likely to be murdered by a current or former partner than by anyone else.

Just determining the number of intimate femicide cases in South Africa is complicated. Police don't record this data because intimate partner violence hasn't been legally defined. Instead, domestic violence is recorded under a range of other categories including assault, malicious damage to property, pointing a firearm and murder.

Beyond the numbers are the stories and to understand those, Dr Shanaaz Mathews spent every week for almost two years visiting prisons. There she spoke to men who had murdered their partners. " I did only one interview each visit because they were really intense

The men chose romantic partners who were young and naive. They put them on a pedestal as the "ideal woman." According to Mathews, they didn't understand that a person can be good and still have flaws. As they got to know their wives or girlfriends, saw their faults and felt disrespected, they would then label their partners as "bad," which, in their minds, allowed them to be violent and to kill. This is one reason women are most at risk if they decide to leave a relationship.
"In their narratives, there's a great sense of betrayal by these women: 'She failed me,'" says Mathews. "None of them take actual ownership of what they did."
Ironically it was Reeva Steenkamp who spoke out against the abuse of women in South Africa. Now her cousin Kim Martin, herself a victim of domestic abuse, is supporting victims of domestic violence through the Reeva Steenkamp foundation.

Lawyers Against Abuse (LvA) operates out of a small trailer in Diepsloot. Shockingly, 56 percent of men in Diepsloot admitted to raping or beating a woman in the past 12 months.
Carte Blanche puts this issue under the spotlight and asks why is nothing working to reduce this heinous crime?

Press Release:


Brutal Legacy
Violence in intimate partner relationships crosses boundaries of wealth and social status. Amid the devastating and ever-spiralling statistics on femicide and a general lack of accountability through the courts, two well-known women shatter the silence that stigma and denial had imposed on them. Carte Blanche scrutinizes how these women were treated by their abusive partners, the police and the courts.


Script:


Brutal Legacy Final Script TX 01. July 2018

Mthunzi Mbuyisa
My mom was the best mom. She was a friend to me, a grandmother, a father too, whenever she was around, you feel her presence, she was the whole world to me, I could say she was my Winnie Mandela

Commentary One
For years, Nomsa Mbuyisa had endured an abusive relationship with the father of her three boys. 18 year old Mthunzi Mbuyisa is her eldest son.

Devi
Mthunzi what was that like for you?
Mthunzi
For me it was like a trauma to see my own dad beating up my own mom. From the first time I saw it was a huge trauma because my mom ended up in hospital she couldn't do anything. She couldn't even move

Devi
Did he ever threaten her with a firearm?
Mthunzi
Every time! He even told my mom, if she wanted to get out of this relationship she would get out dead.

Commentary Two
But Nomsa Mbuyisa did get out, seven months ago she finally cut ties, and moved in with her brother, Dumisani

Devi
So Dumisani, 6 months, it looked like Nomsa had made up her mind.
Dumisani
Everyone in the family was like wow, at least now you took a stand for yourself. She even took all her clothes and gave it to my sister and my mom.
Devi
Why no memories?
Dumisani
She said I don't want memories of this. She even bought a new wardrobe

Commentary three
But on morning of the 30th May, her killer followed Nomsa and Mthunzi as they were about to climb into a taxi. He told Dumisani he wanted to reconcile with Nomsa

Dumisane
I said that won't happen, over my dead body, I am talking to this guy



LINK
And what happened next was so brutal and so shocking, it will remain etched in their memories for the rest of their lives

Mthunzi
My mom was still scratching her purse trying to find the coins. When she was looking down. My dad turned his back against us, acted like he was walking away.

Dumisani
I just heard the gunshot, when I turn my face I see the gun pointing at my sister- he shot her, here

Mthunzi
When he shot my mom for the first time, my brain freezed I couldn't do anything,…I jammed…

Dumisani Mbuyisa
When Nomsa tried to turn her again to hold, he shot her on the chest, when approached he shot me.

Commentary four
The bullet went through Dumisani's leg

Dumisani
After he shot me, he turned the gun to Mthunzi. Mthunzi just hit the gun with his fist, the gun fell on the ground there.

Mthunzi
Everything happened too fast, but I remember he shot my mom three times

Up sound Funeral

Commentary Five
Nomsa Mbuyisa, Transnet employee, breadwinner, mother of three boys, had just become another femicide statistic

3 South African woman a day, die at the hands of their intimate partners. As femicide spikes, frightened women, like Lebo Portia Matee have turned to social media, for help:

"if anything should happen to me tonight, my husband should be a first suspect."

Commentary six
Now, new police minister Bheki Cele has spoken out against this crime, and wants bail denied to abusers



Devi
You have called on the justice cluster to make femicide a schedule 6 offence but what does that mean?
Bheki
If I abuse you and I get bail, I should not get bail for the second abuse, full stop.
Last year we achieved 692 lifers, people that are doing life sentence but the scourge is too big to even to make the impact

Commentary seven
Former newsreader Tracy Going, took many years before she was able to write her story, Brutal legacy.

Tracy
It's taken me 20 years to write the book and I think I needed to reach a place of healing.

Commentary eight
Her story began as a three-year old in Brits, with an alcoholic father

Tracy
My very first childhood memory was as a three-year old standing silently in the dining room watching silently as my father beat my mother.

Commentary nine
Years later, as a successful newsreader, she was returning home from a function with a man she had thought was charming. Then he accused her of telling people he was a drug addict.

Tracy
Why would I do something like that?

Commentary ten
Enraged, he destroyed her garage wall

Tracy
And he pulled me into my house by my hair, undid the phone, locked me in, and kept me hostage for about 8.5 hours.
Devi
What was going through your mind?
Tracy
That was the night I thought I was going to die. I was too scared to scream, I was too scared to say anything. But I got a restraining order on the basis of that incident, and then 3 weeks later he arrived at my home and that was when he beat me up and that was the time I screamed

LINK
Under the domestic violence act, anyone experiencing abusive behavior can ask the court for a protection order, but even that order can fail women if there is little or no enforcement

Commentary eleven
Despite the protection order, her abuser, who Tracy says doesn't deserve to be named, asked if they could get back together again

Tracy
and I said no and that is when he slammed his fist into my face.

Commentary twelve
He also trashed her lounge.

Tracy,
He beat me up, and somehow I managed to get out of his grip as he took a shard of glass from the broken coffee table, and he had it to my face and he said, you need your face and as I realized he was going to cut my face was when I ran outside, and as I got outside he slammed his hand into my back and threw me to the ground and he was running and kicking me

Commentary thirteen
Her neighbours, hearing her screams, pulled her to safety

Devi
But at this stage you had a restraining order?
Tracy
He said to me it's not worth the paper it's written on, and I think he was right, it wasn't worth the paper it was written on

Devi
How many times did Nomsa go to the police Dumisani?
Dumisani
With me present, 10 times
Devi
And what happened when she went
Dumisani
She would lay a charge and they would say no we don't have cars, when we go back on other cases, no we don't have a docket of that case, restart opening a case again
Devi
So the docket would go missing?
Dumisani
Would go missing, yes.

Commentary fourteen
Sometimes Nomsa would withdraw the charges, herself

Devi
Mthunzi, it seems as if your mom, was superwoman in every area of her life but this was her weakness?

Mthunzi
I always felt helpless, because I couldn't save my mom, even on the day she died, I couldn't do anything to save her life

Josina Machel
It was one assault, it happened 30 seconds and in 30 seconds life just changes

Commentary fifteen
Daughter of a president, and Graca Machel, step daughter to Nelson Mandela

Link
Still that privilege offered no safe refuge for Josina Machel on the night of her mother's birthday.

Commentary sixteen
Josina was in the car with her boyfriend. She wanted to go home and spend time with her mother. Her partner at the time, disagreed.

Josina
I was taking my shoes off and all of a sudden, BOOM it's here, and I was so shocked, and I turn, and I look at him and say what and that is when the second blow hits me - hit on my right eye and the eye just burst right there and then

LINK
She managed to get out of the car, holding her eye and ran down the road screaming. No one helped her
Josina
No one came out. No one came out
Devi
What did you do?
Josina
it seems like I fainted

Commentary seventeen
Then her attacker drove towards her, picked her up, and took her to hospital

Josina Machel
The being drives towards me and puts me in the car and at that point I thought I was going to die, I couldn't do anything I just see the lights
Devi
What do you call him?
Josina
The being. Ya it's not a person that does that to you so…I call it
Devi
So you have given IT a name?
Josina
Ya, because it lost its humanity at that point.

Commentary
Machel has now founded an NGO called Khuluka, that will provide shelters for abused women in Mozambique.

LINK
Different countries, different courts, different cases and yet both Tracy and Josina's experiences inside those courts is remarkably similar

Devi
What was the legal process like for you?
Josina
Abuse again! Its abuse all over again!

Tracy
I expected to be heard in the courtroom, but I was completely silenced, my photographs of me being beaten up were waived disparagingly in front of my face, what is this you are completely exaggerating. I was accused of doing it for money, they wanted to paint a picture of me as this volatile, hysterical woman

Devi
Did you often feel like you were being tried here?
Josina
Oh ya, ya, ya! because all of a sudden, you're lying, you are fabricating evidence, your credibility is on the line and I and I think if you lose your eye …just being beaten up is humiliating enough. What do you gain with that

Commentary eighteen
Like many women, evidence also went missing in her case

Josina
You have to prove you were in the hospital, you have to prove you were at the police. So, we get to the police there was no record
Devi
But Josina your father was the president of the country - your file should not have gone missing?
Josina
It did.
Devi
What does it say for women whose father is not the president
Josina
Exactly and it happened to me in order to show the world what happens to every single woman in these kind of situations

Commentary nineteen
Her abuser is appealing his sentence, a process Josina says can take ten years.
Josina
He was found guilty, he got a suspended sentence, and there was the compensation
Devi
Has he paid
Josina
Not one cent

Tracy
I don't believe I got justice, he got a one -year sentence suspended for 5 years and small monetary fine. The magistrate was completely sympathetic, the chauvinism in the court room it was definitely, them against us. He found it was an isolated incident through provocation

Commentary Twenty
Nomsa Mbuyisa's killer, was arrested but the family are skeptical they will get justice, and asked a sangoma to put a curse on him

Up sound Funeral

Mthunzi Mbuyisa
I am the last person to see her lying there down. It hurts me, I can't even describe the feeling because the feeling is unbearable
Devi
Mthunzi if there was one thing What would you say to your mom.
Mthunzi
I promise to finish my studies. I promise to look after her kids. I promise to make her dreams come true. I promise to leave her legacy
Devi
And you Dumisani
Dumisani
I love you. I would say I love you.

THE END DURATION 12 minutes.


PROMO ONE 10 seconds
Three South African women per day are killed by their intimate partners
Mthunzi
When he shot my mom for the first time, my brain freezed I couldn't do anything, I jammed…

PROMO TWO 15 seconds
In 2015 Josina Machel, daughter of a president and Graca machel, was assaulted by her former partner.

Josina Machel
It was one assault, it happened 30 seconds and in 30 seconds life just changes





PROMO THREE 15 seconds
former news reader Tracy Going took 20 years before she was ready to tell her story of abuse.

Tracy
he took a shard of glass from the broken coffee table, and he had it to my face and he said, you need your face


PROMO FOUR 30seconds
Commentary
Graca Machel's daughter, Josina Machel shares her story as a survivor of intimate partner violence

Josina
You have to prove you were in the hospital, you have to prove you were at the police. So, we get to the police there was no record
Devi
But Josina your father was the president of the country - your file should not have gone missing?
Josina
It did.
Devi
What does it say for women whose father is not the president
Josina
Exactly! Exactly!

Tracy, He beat me up, and somehow I managed to get out of his grip as he took a shard of glass from the broken coffee table, and he had it to my face and he said, you need your face and as I realized he was going to cut my face was when I ran outside, and as I got outside he slammed his hand into my back and threw me to the ground and he was running and kicking me Commentary thirteen Her neighbours, hearing her screams, pulled her to safety Devi But at this stage you had a restraining order? Tracy He said to me it's not worth the paper it's written on, and I think he was right, it wasn't worth the paper it was written on Devi How many times did Nomsa go to the police Dumisani? Dumisani With me present, 10 times Devi And what happened when she went Dumisani She would lay a charge and they would say no we don't have cars, when we go back on other cases, no we don't have a docket of that case, restart opening a case again Devi So the docket would go missing? Dumisani Would go missing, yes. Commentary fourteen Sometimes Nomsa would withdraw the charges, herself Devi Mthunzi, it seems as if your mom, was superwoman in every area of her life but this was her weakness? Mthunzi I always felt helpless, because I couldn't save my mom, even on the day she died, I couldn't do anything to save her life Josina Machel It was one assault, it happened 30 seconds and in 30 seconds life just changes Commentary fifteen Daughter of a president, and Graca Machel, step daughter to Nelson Mandela Link Still that privilege offered no safe refuge for Josina Machel on the night of her mother's birthday. Commentary sixteen Josina was in the car with her boyfriend. She wanted to go home and spend time with her mother. Her partner at the time, disagreed. Josina I was taking my shoes off and all of a sudden, BOOM it's here, and I was so shocked, and I turn, and I look at him and say what and that is when the second blow hits me - hit on my right eye and the eye just burst right there and then LINK She managed to get out of the car, holding her eye and ran down the road screaming. No one helped her Josina No one came out. No one came out Devi What did you do? Josina it seems like I fainted Commentary seventeen Then her attacker drove towards her, picked her up, and took her to hospital Josina Machel The being drives towards me and puts me in the car and at that point I thought I was going to die, I couldn't do anything I just see the lights Devi What do you call him? Josina The being. Ya it's not a person that does that to you so…I call it Devi So you have given IT a name? Josina Ya, because it lost its humanity at that point. Commentary Machel has now founded an NGO called Khuluka, that will provide shelters for abused women in Mozambique. LINK Different countries, different courts, different cases and yet both Tracy and Josina's experiences inside those courts is remarkably similar Devi What was the legal process like for you? Josina Abuse again! Its abuse all over again! Tracy I expected to be heard in the courtroom, but I was completely silenced, my photographs of me being beaten up were waived disparagingly in front of my face, what is this you are completely exaggerating. I was accused of doing it for money, they wanted to paint a picture of me as this volatile, hysterical woman Devi Did you often feel like you were being tried here? Josina Oh ya, ya, ya! because all of a sudden, you're lying, you are fabricating evidence, your credibility is on the line and I and I think if you lose your eye …just being beaten up is humiliating enough. What do you gain with that Commentary eighteen Like many women, evidence also went missing in her case Josina You have to prove you were in the hospital, you have to prove you were at the police. So, we get to the police there was no record Devi But Josina your father was the president of the country - your file should not have gone missing? Josina It did. Devi What does it say for women whose father is not the president Josina Exactly and it happened to me in order to show the world what happens to every single woman in these kind of situations Commentary nineteen Her abuser is appealing his sentence, a process Josina says can take ten years. Josina He was found guilty, he got a suspended sentence, and there was the compensation Devi Has he paid Josina Not one cent Tracy I don't believe I got justice, he got a one -year sentence suspended for 5 years and small monetary fine. The magistrate was completely sympathetic, the chauvinism in the court room it was definitely, them against us. He found it was an isolated incident through provocation Commentary Twenty Nomsa Mbuyisa's killer, was arrested but the family are skeptical they will get justice, and asked a sangoma to put a curse on him Up sound Funeral Mthunzi Mbuyisa I am the last person to see her lying there down. It hurts me, I can't even describe the feeling because the feeling is unbearable Devi Mthunzi if there was one thing What would you say to your mom. Mthunzi I promise to finish my studies. I promise to look after her kids. I promise to make her dreams come true. I promise to leave her legacy Devi And you Dumisani Dumisani I love you. I would say I love you. THE END DURATION 12 minutes. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): the biggest threat to South African women come from their own partners. Why cant South Africa reduce stop this terrible crime
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Powerful personal stories well told. Footage from the Oscar Trial - startling statistics. Unsung heroines
metadata.Summary: "As I stood before him all I could see were the lies, the disappearing for days without warning, the screaming, the threats, the terror, the hostage-holding, the keeping me up all night, the dragging me through the house by my hair, the choking, the doors locked around me, the phones disconnected, the isolation, the fear and the uncertainty." A new book, Brutal Legacy, by former newsreader Tracy Going tells about the night she thought she would die at the hands of her partner. The book comes at a time that Karabo Mokoena's partner stands trial for her murder and Constantia business man Rob Packham is accused of murdering his wife Gill. Both women's bodies found, charred beyond recognition.
metadata.Further information: Tracy Going survived the attack when neighbours intervened, but the scars remained. When Oscar killed his girlfriend Reeva, Tracy spent obsessive hours watching the channel and came close to a nervous breakdown. To heal herself she began to write her story. It is a searing account of abuse in the home, first by first her father and later her partner "I was ashamed of my father, the drunk. If he wasn't throwing back the liquid in the lounge then he'd be finding comfort and consort in his cans at the golf club. With that came the uncertainty as I lay in my bed and waited for him to return. I would lie there holding my curtain tight in my small hand. I would pull the fabric down, almost straight, forming a strained sliver and I would peer into the blackness, unblinking. It seemed I was always watching and waiting. Sometimes I searched for satellites between the twinkles of light, but mostly the fear in my tummy distracted me." One woman every eight hours dies at the hands of her partner. In Canada for example its one every six days. Despite nearly 20 years of government legislation and awareness campaigns to reduce domestic violence, South African women are still more likely to be murdered by a current or former partner than by anyone else. Just determining the number of intimate femicide cases in South Africa is complicated. Police don't record this data because intimate partner violence hasn't been legally defined. Instead, domestic violence is recorded under a range of other categories including assault, malicious damage to property, pointing a firearm and murder. Beyond the numbers are the stories and to understand those, Dr Shanaaz Mathews spent every week for almost two years visiting prisons. There she spoke to men who had murdered their partners. " I did only one interview each visit because they were really intense The men chose romantic partners who were young and naive. They put them on a pedestal as the "ideal woman." According to Mathews, they didn't understand that a person can be good and still have flaws. As they got to know their wives or girlfriends, saw their faults and felt disrespected, they would then label their partners as "bad," which, in their minds, allowed them to be violent and to kill. This is one reason women are most at risk if they decide to leave a relationship. "In their narratives, there's a great sense of betrayal by these women: 'She failed me,'" says Mathews. "None of them take actual ownership of what they did." Ironically it was Reeva Steenkamp who spoke out against the abuse of women in South Africa. Now her cousin Kim Martin, herself a victim of domestic abuse, is supporting victims of domestic violence through the Reeva Steenkamp foundation. Lawyers Against Abuse (LvA) operates out of a small trailer in Diepsloot. Shockingly, 56 percent of men in Diepsloot admitted to raping or beating a woman in the past 12 months. Carte Blanche puts this issue under the spotlight and asks why is nothing working to reduce this heinous crime?
